newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition calls for 'passive resistance'.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition calls for 'passive resistance'.

text.p: Serbia's opposition has called for a public campaign of passive resistance after the autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic ordered his riot police to forcibly break up pro-democracy protests.

"We must all turn into a great river of non-violent resistance," opposition politician Vuk Draskovic told cheering, whistling supporters in downtown Belgrade on Monday. "All schools and faculties must close, we must not pay any taxes and bills and we must all go on strike."

The call for a Gandhi-style revolt followed the most aggressive police action seen in Serbia for years, with anti-riot police repeatedly charging largely peaceful protesters on Sunday night. At least 100 people were injured.

On Monday, 77th straight day of rallies demanding reinstatement of opposition victories in local elections last November, young militants hurled stones at police, provoking what witnesses said were indiscriminate beatings.

Initially, 80,000 people turned out to confront police and the vast majority dispersed quietly when asked to do so by their political leaders, but about 200 youths ranged through the streets in a cat-and-mouse game with heavily-armed police.

The violence prompted international denunciations of Milosevic's "get tough" policy, with Washington protesting to Serbia and strongly condemning "the most serious use of force" against the demonstrators.
The French government, in a policy shift, invited leaders of three-party Zajedno opposition alliance to Paris.

The Serbian Interior Ministry issued a statement saying 18 people were arrested on Sunday night and that it would continue to take all necessary measures "with the goal of preventing threats to public transport and public order, peace and security of citizens..."
Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader, echoed the call for continued non-violent protest, saying people were more determined than ever in pressing for change.

"You must not let yourselves be drawn into a fight with the police, because you will be on their ground -- they have the physical force, but the stamina, morale, truth, international support and justice are on our side."
More than 1,000 schools are shut, lawyers have rallied with students, churchmen and senior soldiers have backed opposition demands for election results to be reinstated.

Belgrade's popular film festival, an annual event, has been suspended after foreign distributors withdrew their films within days of the opening. Most theatres and cinemas in the capital have also shut down.
Milosevic, meanwhile, had other concerns on Monday.
Tanjug news agency said he congratulated leading Interior Ministry officials following a successful "anti-terrorist operation" in Serbian-ruled Kosovo province.

The operation took place between January 22 and 29 and resulted in the arrests of 66 "members of terrorist organisations... among them perpetrators of terrorist acts carried out in Kosovo," Tanjug said.
Serbian police had shot dead three ethnic Albanians in a gun battle on Friday as part of an operation aimed at stamping out "terrorism", the agency said.
A suspected commander of the shadowy Kosovo Liberation Army was one of those killed.
But the region's main political party, the Democratic League, has criticised the killings as part of a brutal crackdown on ethnic Albanian political activists and humanitarian workers.

In Sarajevo, Bosnia's co-prime minister, Haris Silajdzic, told a news conference he was concerned that Milosevic might try to divert attention from the Belgrade protests by stirring up conflict in the predominantly ethnic Albanian region.
"If that happens, I think the whole region is in danger. So long as the regime in Belgrade is in place, the entire area will not enjoy peace," he said.
